claims.text: Compositionally complex alloys or high-entropy alloys are inherently resistant to temper embrittlement.
Compositionally complex alloys or high-entropy alloys can be used to produce a ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
Resistance to temper embrittlement enables the proposed ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
Exposure to a range of temperatures will induce a ductile–brittle–ductile transition in the alloy.
Conventional alloys exhibit temper embrittlement over the specified temperature range.
A complex, multicomponent alloy composition hinders the formation of embrittling phases.
The alloy composition suppresses impurity segregation.
The alloy composition suppresses the formation of brittle phases.
Suppression of impurity segregation and brittle-phase formation maintains ductility across the temperature range.
The alloy will exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition without the dramatic loss of ductility associated with temper embrittlement.
The behavior may vary with alloy composition and processing history.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts induction of a brittle intermediate state while also claiming that the mechanism maintains ductility across the temperature range and that no dramatic ductility loss occurs. The property change defining the proposed brittle state is therefore unclear.

Resistance to temper embrittlement is presented as the reason for a ductile–brittle–ductile transition, but suppression of embrittlement would ordinarily explain the absence of a brittle interval rather than its occurrence.
